## DD001

**Base image has no tag or uses :latest**  
`unpinned-base-image` · warn · reproducibility · Dockerfile

A FROM line without a tag, or with :latest, points at whatever the registry calls "newest" on the day you build.

**Why it matters.** Two builds of the same commit can produce different images. A rebuild at 2 a.m. can pull a new major version of your runtime and break production with no change in your repo. Pin a specific version, then update it on purpose.

Before:

```dockerfile
FROM node
FROM python:latest
```

After:

```dockerfile
FROM node:22.11-alpine3.20
FROM python:3.12-slim-bookworm
```

## DD002

**Base image is tagged but not pinned by digest**  
`base-image-no-digest` · info · reproducibility · Dockerfile

A version tag such as node:22.11-alpine can still be re-pushed by the publisher. A digest (@sha256:...) cannot.

**Why it matters.** Tags are mutable. If you need bit-for-bit repeatable builds or want to prove which base you shipped, pin the digest and let a bot (Dependabot, Renovate) bump it. This is informational because digests make Dockerfiles harder to read.

Before:

```dockerfile
FROM node:22.11-alpine3.20
```

After:

```dockerfile
FROM node:22.11-alpine3.20@sha256:<digest>
```

## DD003

**Container runs as root (no USER instruction)**  
`run-as-root` · warn · security · Dockerfile

The final stage never sets USER, so the process runs as uid 0 inside the container. Base images that already default to a non-root user (distroless :nonroot, *-unprivileged, Chainguard, Bitnami) are not reported.

**Why it matters.** If the app has a remote-code-execution bug, the attacker starts as root inside the container, which makes breakouts, writes to mounted volumes and abuse of the container runtime far easier. A fixed non-root uid costs one line.

Before:

```dockerfile
FROM node:22-alpine
COPY . /app
CMD ["node", "/app/server.js"]
```

After:

```dockerfile
FROM node:22-alpine
COPY --chown=node:node . /app
USER node
CMD ["node", "/app/server.js"]
```

## DD004

**The last USER in the final stage is root**  
`explicit-root-user` · warn · security · Dockerfile

The final stage switches to root (USER root, USER 0) and never switches back to an unprivileged user.

**Why it matters.** Same risk as having no USER at all, but written down on purpose. Switching to root to install packages is fine as long as the stage ends with a non-root USER.

Before:

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-slim
USER root
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
```

After:

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-slim
RUN useradd --system --uid 10001 app
USER app
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
```

## DD005

**ADD used where COPY would do**  
`add-instead-of-copy` · warn · maintainability · Dockerfile · auto-fixable

ADD has hidden behaviour: it fetches URLs and auto-extracts local tar archives. When you only want to copy files into the image, COPY says exactly that and nothing more.

**Why it matters.** A file that happens to be a tarball gets silently unpacked, and a URL gets downloaded without a checksum. COPY is predictable and easier to review.

Before:

```dockerfile
ADD ./config /etc/app/
```

After:

```dockerfile
COPY ./config /etc/app/
```

## DD006

**ADD downloads a URL without a checksum**  
`add-remote-url` · warn · security · Dockerfile

ADD <url> downloads at build time and trusts whatever comes back. Without --checksum the content is not verified.

**Why it matters.** A compromised or changed download is baked into your image and into every layer cache after it. Verify what you download.

Before:

```dockerfile
ADD https://example.com/tool-1.2.tar.gz /tmp/
```

After:

```dockerfile
ADD --checksum=sha256:<digest> https://example.com/tool-1.2.tar.gz /tmp/
# or: RUN curl -fsSLO <url> && echo "<digest>  file" | sha256sum -c -
```

## DD007

**Remote script piped straight into a shell**  
`curl-pipe-shell` · error · security · Dockerfile

A RUN step downloads with curl or wget and pipes the result into sh, bash or an interpreter in one go.

**Why it matters.** You execute code you never read, as root, and a truncated download can run a half-written script. Download the file, check its checksum or signature, then run it.

Before:

```dockerfile
RUN curl -sSL https://example.com/install.sh | sh
```

After:

```dockerfile
RUN curl -fsSLo /tmp/install.sh https://example.com/install.sh \
 && echo "<sha256>  /tmp/install.sh" | sha256sum -c - \
 && sh /tmp/install.sh
```

## DD008

**Secret-looking ENV/ARG with a literal value**  
`secret-in-env-arg` · error · security · Dockerfile

An ENV or ARG whose name looks like a credential (PASSWORD, TOKEN, API_KEY, ...) is given a literal value. ARG without a default and ENV copied from an ARG are reported as warnings.

**Why it matters.** ENV values live in the image config and ARG values are recorded in `docker history`. Anyone who can pull the image can read them, and rotating the secret means rebuilding every image. Pass secrets at runtime, or use BuildKit secret mounts for build-time needs.

Before:

```dockerfile
ENV DB_PASSWORD=hunter2
ARG NPM_TOKEN
```

After:

```dockerfile
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npm_token \
    NPM_TOKEN=$(cat /run/secrets/npm_token) npm ci
```

## DD009

**Value matches a known credential format or looks like a random token**  
`secret-pattern` · error · security · Dockerfile

Text in the Dockerfile matches a well-known credential shape (AWS access key id, GitHub/Slack/Stripe token, private key block, JWT, user:password in a URL) or an ENV/ARG value is a long high-entropy string.

**Why it matters.** Credentials committed to a Dockerfile are in your git history and in every image built from it. Treat anything reported here as already leaked: rotate it, then remove it.

Before:

```dockerfile
ENV AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE
RUN git clone https://ci:s3cr3tpass@git.example.com/app.git
```

After:

```dockerfile
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=git_creds \
    git clone https://git.example.com/app.git
```

## DD010

**sudo or su used inside a RUN step**  
`sudo-or-su` · warn · security · Dockerfile

RUN steps already execute as the current USER (root by default). sudo and su add nothing during a build.

**Why it matters.** Installing sudo adds a setuid binary to the image, and `su`/`sudo` at runtime is a privilege-escalation path. Use USER to switch identities and run privileged build steps before the switch.

Before:

```dockerfile
RUN sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y curl
```

After:

```dockerfile
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl
```

## DD011

**chmod makes files world-writable**  
`chmod-world-writable` · warn · security · Dockerfile

chmod 777 (or o+w, a+rwx, --chmod=777) lets every user in the container modify the files.

**Why it matters.** It is almost always a shortcut to silence a permissions error. Any compromised process in the container can then rewrite your code or config. Fix the owner (chown / USER) and grant only what is needed.

Before:

```dockerfile
RUN chmod -R 777 /app
```

After:

```dockerfile
RUN chown -R app:app /app && chmod -R u=rwX,go=rX /app
```

## DD012

**EXPOSE 22 (SSH) in an application image**  
`expose-ssh-port` · warn · security · Dockerfile

The image declares port 22, which is SSH.

**Why it matters.** Running an SSH daemon inside a container is almost never needed (use `docker exec`, `kubectl exec` or a bastion) and it adds a login surface, host keys and credentials to manage.

Before:

```dockerfile
EXPOSE 22 8080
```

After:

```dockerfile
EXPOSE 8080
```

## DD013

**Privileged port (<1024) exposed by a non-root image**  
`expose-privileged-port` · info · correctness · Dockerfile

The image runs as a non-root USER but exposes a port below 1024, which unprivileged processes usually cannot bind (Kubernetes and rootless runtimes do not relax this).

**Why it matters.** The app works on a laptop and then fails to start in the cluster with "permission denied". Listen on 8080/8443 and map it at the edge.

Before:

```dockerfile
USER app
EXPOSE 80
```

After:

```dockerfile
USER app
EXPOSE 8080
```

## DD014

**COPY/ADD of a credentials or key file**  
`sensitive-file-copied` · error · security · Dockerfile

A COPY or ADD names a file that normally holds secrets: .env, SSH or TLS private keys, .npmrc/.pypirc, cloud credentials, kubeconfig, the .git directory, Terraform state.

**Why it matters.** Files copied into a layer stay there even if you delete them in a later step. Anyone with the image can extract them. Mount secrets at build time instead of copying them.

Before:

```dockerfile
COPY .env /app/.env
COPY id_rsa /root/.ssh/
```

After:

```dockerfile
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=ssh,target=/root/.ssh/id_rsa git clone git@example.com:org/repo.git
```

## DD015

**TLS or signature checking switched off**  
`insecure-transport` · warn · security · Dockerfile

A build step disables certificate or signature verification: curl -k, wget --no-check-certificate, pip --trusted-host, apt --allow-unauthenticated, git http.sslVerify=false, NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0, and similar.

**Why it matters.** It turns every download in the build into something a network attacker can swap. Fix the trust store (install the CA certificate) rather than turning verification off.

Before:

```dockerfile
RUN curl -k https://internal.example.com/pkg.tgz -o pkg.tgz
```

After:

```dockerfile
COPY corp-ca.crt /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/
RUN update-ca-certificates \
 && curl -fsSL https://internal.example.com/pkg.tgz -o pkg.tgz
```

## DD016

**apt-get update runs in a different RUN than apt-get install**  
`apt-update-not-combined` · warn · reproducibility · Dockerfile

apt-get update is in its own RUN instruction, with no install in the same step.

**Why it matters.** Docker caches each RUN layer. The "update" layer is cached forever while later "install" layers change, so a new package is installed against a stale package index and fails with 404s, or installs old versions. Keep update and install in one RUN.

Before:

```dockerfile
RUN apt-get update
RUN apt-get install -y curl
```

After:

```dockerfile
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl
```

## DD017

**`apt` used in a script instead of `apt-get`**  
`apt-cli-unstable` · info · maintainability · Dockerfile · auto-fixable

`apt` is the interactive front end. Its output and options are not guaranteed stable for scripts; apt-get is.

**Why it matters.** apt prints "WARNING: apt does not have a stable CLI interface" on every build and may change behaviour between releases.

Before:

```dockerfile
RUN apt update && apt install -y curl
```

After:

```dockerfile
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl
```

## DD018

**pip / npm -g / gem install without a version**  
`unpinned-package-install` · info · reproducibility · Dockerfile

Packages named directly on the command line (pip install flask, npm install -g typescript, gem install rails) have no version pin.

**Why it matters.** The same Dockerfile installs different versions next month. Pin the version (flask==3.0.3) or install from a lock file.

Before:

```dockerfile
RUN pip install flask gunicorn
RUN npm install -g typescript
```

After:

```dockerfile
RUN pip install flask==3.0.3 gunicorn==22.0.0
RUN npm install -g typescript@5.6.3
```

## DD019

**npm install / yarn / pnpm install without a frozen lock file**  
`npm-install-not-ci` · warn · reproducibility · Dockerfile

`npm install` may rewrite package-lock.json and pick newer versions inside your ranges. `npm ci` installs exactly what the lock file says. The same applies to yarn without --frozen-lockfile (--immutable on Berry) and pnpm install without --frozen-lockfile.

**Why it matters.** Builds stop being repeatable: a transitive dependency released an hour ago ends up in production. `npm ci` is also faster and fails loudly when package.json and the lock file disagree.

Before:

```dockerfile
RUN npm install
```

After:

```dockerfile
RUN npm ci
```

## DD020

**COPY . . comes before the dependency install (busts the layer cache)**  
`copy-all-before-install` · warn · maintainability · Dockerfile

The whole source tree is copied before the step that installs dependencies. Any edit to any file invalidates the install layer.

**Why it matters.** Every build re-downloads all dependencies even when only one source line changed. Copy only the manifest and lock file first, install, then copy the rest. CI minutes and developer patience are both saved.

Before:

```dockerfile
COPY . .
RUN npm ci
```

After:

```dockerfile
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
```

## DD021

**ARG used outside the scope where it is defined**  
`arg-scope` · warn · correctness · Dockerfile

An ARG declared before the first FROM is only visible to FROM lines. Inside a stage it is empty unless you repeat `ARG NAME` after FROM. Build-platform ARGs such as TARGETARCH behave the same way.

**Why it matters.** The build does not fail: the variable silently expands to an empty string, so you get a wrong path, a missing version or a broken download URL that only shows up at runtime.

Before:

```dockerfile
ARG APP_VERSION=1.4.0
FROM alpine:3.20
LABEL version=$APP_VERSION
```

After:

```dockerfile
ARG APP_VERSION=1.4.0
FROM alpine:3.20
ARG APP_VERSION
LABEL version=$APP_VERSION
```

## DD022

**Duplicate stage name or COPY --from pointing at a stage that does not exist yet**  
`stage-reference` · error · correctness · Dockerfile

Stage names must be unique, and COPY --from=<stage> can only refer to an earlier stage. A name that is one typo away from a real stage is reported too.

**Why it matters.** A wrong --from either fails the build late (after the slow compile steps) or, worse, quietly pulls an unrelated public image with that name from Docker Hub.

Before:

```dockerfile
FROM golang:1.23 AS build
FROM alpine:3.20
COPY --from=biuld /out/app /app
```

After:

```dockerfile
FROM golang:1.23 AS build
FROM alpine:3.20
COPY --from=build /out/app /app
```

## DD023

**apt-get upgrade / apk upgrade / yum update in an image build**  
`package-upgrade-all` · warn · reproducibility · Dockerfile

The build upgrades every installed package instead of installing the ones you need.

**Why it matters.** The result depends on the day you build, and it hides the real fix: choose a newer, patched base image. Rebuild on a schedule against a pinned base instead.

Before:

```dockerfile
RUN apt-get update && apt-get -y upgrade
```

After:

```dockerfile
FROM debian:12.7-slim   # bump this when security updates land
```

## DD024

**apt-get install without --no-install-recommends**  
`apt-no-install-recommends` · warn · size · Dockerfile · auto-fixable

apt installs "recommended" packages by default, which are often large and unrelated to what you asked for.

**Why it matters.** Images routinely shrink by tens or hundreds of megabytes, and the attack surface shrinks with them. Reported for stages that end up in the final image.

Before:

```dockerfile
RUN apt-get install -y curl
```

After:

```dockerfile
RUN apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl
```

## DD025

**apt package lists are left in the layer**  
`apt-lists-not-cleaned` · warn · size · Dockerfile · auto-fixable

The RUN that runs apt-get install does not delete /var/lib/apt/lists/* in the same step.

**Why it matters.** The package index (tens of MB) is stored in the layer forever; deleting it in a later RUN does not shrink the image because layers only add. Clean in the same RUN.

Before:

```dockerfile
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl
```

After:

```dockerfile
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
```

## DD026

**pip install without --no-cache-dir**  
`pip-no-cache-dir` · warn · size · Dockerfile · auto-fixable

pip keeps downloaded wheels in ~/.cache/pip, which ends up in the image layer.

**Why it matters.** The cache is never used again inside the image, but it can add 50-300 MB. Use --no-cache-dir (or set PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=1, or use a BuildKit cache mount).

Before:

```dockerfile
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
```

After:

```dockerfile
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
```

## DD027

**apk add without --no-cache**  
`apk-no-cache` · warn · size · Dockerfile · auto-fixable

apk add stores the package index under /var/cache/apk unless you pass --no-cache.

**Why it matters.** --no-cache fetches the index on the fly and leaves nothing behind, so there is no separate `apk update` and no cleanup step to forget.

Before:

```dockerfile
RUN apk update && apk add curl
```

After:

```dockerfile
RUN apk add --no-cache curl
```

## DD028

**Compilers or build headers are installed in the image that ships**  
`build-tools-in-final-stage` · warn · size · Dockerfile

The shipped stage installs gcc, make, build-essential, *-dev headers or similar and does not remove them in the same step. This is the single-stage-build smell.

**Why it matters.** Toolchains add hundreds of MB and give an attacker a compiler inside your container. Build in a separate stage and copy the result, or install the toolchain as a virtual package and delete it in the same RUN.

Before:

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.12
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y build-essential libpq-dev
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
```

After:

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.12 AS build
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y build-essential libpq-dev
RUN pip wheel -r requirements.txt -w /wheels
FROM python:3.12-slim
COPY --from=build /wheels /wheels
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir /wheels/*
```

## DD029

**Development dependencies are installed into the image that ships**  
`dev-deps-in-final-stage` · warn · size · Dockerfile

npm/yarn/pnpm install without --omit=dev (or NODE_ENV=production), composer install without --no-dev, uv sync without --no-dev, poetry install without --only main, pip -r requirements-dev.txt: in a stage that ends up in the final image.

**Why it matters.** Test runners, linters, type checkers and bundlers inflate the image and widen the attack surface. Install dev dependencies only in the build stage.

Before:

```dockerfile
FROM node:22-alpine
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
```

After:

```dockerfile
FROM node:22-alpine
ENV NODE_ENV=production
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
```

## DD030

**COPY . with no .dockerignore next to the Dockerfile**  
`missing-dockerignore` · warn · size · Dockerfile

The Dockerfile copies the whole build context (COPY . ., ADD . ., COPY * ...) but no .dockerignore (or <Dockerfile>.dockerignore) exists. Only reported when the file is scanned from disk.

**Why it matters.** Without it, .git, node_modules, local .env files, test data and editor junk are sent to the daemon and copied into the image. That makes builds slow, images big, and can leak secrets.

Before:

```dockerfile
# repo has no .dockerignore
COPY . /app
```

After:

```dockerfile
# .dockerignore
.git
node_modules
.env
*.log
```

## DD031

**ENV DEBIAN_FRONTEND leaks into the running container**  
`debian-frontend-env` · info · correctness · Dockerfile

ENV DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive is set for the life of the image, not just the install step.

**Why it matters.** Anyone who later runs apt inside the container gets silently non-interactive behaviour. Scope it to the RUN, or use ARG (build-time only).

Before:

```dockerfile
ENV DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive
```

After:

```dockerfile
ARG DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive
```

## DD032

**Final image defines no HEALTHCHECK**  
`no-healthcheck` · info · correctness · Dockerfile

No HEALTHCHECK instruction is present in the final stage (or the stages it is built on).

**Why it matters.** Docker, Compose and Swarm can only restart or route around a hung process if the image says how to test health. Kubernetes ignores HEALTHCHECK and uses probes, so this is informational: batch jobs and k8s-only images can ignore it.

Before:

```dockerfile
FROM nginx:1.27-alpine
```

After:

```dockerfile
FROM nginx:1.27-alpine
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s CMD wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1/ || exit 1
```

## DD033

**WORKDIR is a relative path**  
`workdir-relative` · warn · correctness · Dockerfile

WORKDIR is relative and there is no earlier absolute WORKDIR in the stage to anchor it.

**Why it matters.** A relative WORKDIR resolves against whatever directory the base image happens to start in. That differs between images and between versions of the same image.

Before:

```dockerfile
WORKDIR app
```

After:

```dockerfile
WORKDIR /app
```

## DD034

**CMD / ENTRYPOINT in shell form**  
`shell-form-cmd` · warn · correctness · Dockerfile · auto-fixable

CMD and ENTRYPOINT written as plain text run through `/bin/sh -c`, so the shell, not your app, becomes PID 1. The JSON (exec) form starts your process directly. A trivial command is rewritten automatically by --fix.

**Why it matters.** Signals (SIGTERM from `docker stop` or Kubernetes) go to the shell and are not forwarded, so the app never shuts down gracefully and is killed after the timeout (10 s by default). Exec form fixes that and removes a process from the container.

Before:

```dockerfile
CMD node server.js
```

After:

```dockerfile
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

## DD035

**More than one CMD, ENTRYPOINT or HEALTHCHECK in a stage**  
`multiple-cmd-entrypoint` · warn · correctness · Dockerfile

Only the last CMD, ENTRYPOINT and HEALTHCHECK in a stage take effect. Earlier ones are silently ignored.

**Why it matters.** It usually means a line was pasted twice or a base-stage instruction was forgotten, and the container starts something other than what the file reads like.

Before:

```dockerfile
CMD ["npm", "start"]
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

After:

```dockerfile
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

## DD036

**COPY after USER without --chown (files stay owned by root)**  
`copy-missing-chown` · info · security · Dockerfile

After a non-root USER, COPY/ADD still creates files owned by root unless you pass --chown. Only the first occurrence per stage is reported.

**Why it matters.** Read-only code owned by root is fine, and even preferable. But if the app needs to write next to the copied files (caches, uploads, SQLite, compiled templates) it fails at runtime with "permission denied". Decide on purpose: --chown for writable paths, root ownership for read-only ones.

Before:

```dockerfile
USER app
COPY . /app
```

After:

```dockerfile
USER app
COPY --chown=app:app . /app
```

## DD037

**MAINTAINER is deprecated**  
`maintainer-deprecated` · warn · maintainability · Dockerfile · auto-fixable

The MAINTAINER instruction has been deprecated for years. Use a LABEL with the standard OCI key instead.

**Why it matters.** LABEL is machine-readable by registries and tooling, and can carry more than a name. --fix rewrites it for you.

Before:

```dockerfile
MAINTAINER Jane Doe <jane@example.com>
```

After:

```dockerfile
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.authors="Jane Doe <jane@example.com>"
```

## DD038

**Exec form looks like JSON but is not valid JSON**  
`invalid-json-form` · error · correctness · Dockerfile

An instruction starts with [ and ends with ] but is not a valid JSON array of strings (single quotes, trailing comma, unquoted words). Docker then falls back to shell form.

**Why it matters.** CMD ['npm', 'start'] is run as the shell command `[ npm, start ]`, which fails at runtime with "[: not found" or silently does nothing. The error appears only when the container starts.

Before:

```dockerfile
CMD ['node', 'server.js']
```

After:

```dockerfile
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

## DD039

**Unknown Dockerfile instruction**  
`unknown-instruction` · error · correctness · Dockerfile

A line begins with a word that is not a Dockerfile instruction. The usual causes are a typo (RNU) or a missing backslash at the end of the previous RUN line.

**Why it matters.** docker build fails with "unknown instruction". A missing line continuation is especially easy to miss in review because the next line looks like part of the command.

Before:

```dockerfile
RUN apt-get update
 && apt-get install -y curl
```

After:

```dockerfile
RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y curl
```

## DD040

**Instruction before the first FROM, or no FROM at all**  
`from-not-first` · error · correctness · Dockerfile

Only ARG (and parser directives or comments) may come before the first FROM. A Dockerfile with no FROM is not a buildable Dockerfile.

**Why it matters.** docker build rejects the file. In a linter pipeline this usually means the wrong file was picked up, or a stray line was pasted at the top.

Before:

```dockerfile
RUN echo hi
FROM alpine:3.20
```

After:

```dockerfile
FROM alpine:3.20
RUN echo hi
```

## DD041

**COPY/ADD with several sources needs a destination ending in /**  
`copy-multi-dest-slash` · error · correctness · Dockerfile

When COPY or ADD has more than one source, the destination must be a directory and end with a slash.

**Why it matters.** The build fails with "When using COPY with more than one source file, the destination must be a directory and end with a /".

Before:

```dockerfile
COPY package.json package-lock.json /app
```

After:

```dockerfile
COPY package.json package-lock.json /app/
```

## DD042

**EXPOSE with an invalid port or protocol**  
`invalid-expose` · error · correctness · Dockerfile

EXPOSE takes port numbers 1-65535, optionally a range and /tcp, /udp or /sctp.

**Why it matters.** docker build rejects it, or the value is ignored by tooling that parses image metadata.

Before:

```dockerfile
EXPOSE 80800
EXPOSE http
```

After:

```dockerfile
EXPOSE 8080
```

## DD043

**Instruction keywords mix upper and lower case**  
`instruction-case` · info · maintainability · Dockerfile · auto-fixable

Some instructions are upper-case and others are not. Docker accepts both, but the convention is upper-case, and a mixed file is harder to scan. Reported only when the file is inconsistent.

**Why it matters.** Consistent keywords make instructions stand out from the commands inside them, which is most of what a Dockerfile reviewer looks at.

Before:

```dockerfile
FROM alpine:3.20
run echo hello
```

After:

```dockerfile
FROM alpine:3.20
RUN echo hello
```

## DD044

**Pipeline in RUN without pipefail**  
`pipe-without-pipefail` · warn · correctness · Dockerfile

A RUN pipes one command into another, but the shell is not set to fail when the first command fails. Pipelines made only of echo/printf/cat are ignored.

**Why it matters.** By default a pipeline succeeds if the last command succeeds. `curl http://broken | tar xz` exits 0 when curl fails, and the build carries on with a half-empty image.

Before:

```dockerfile
RUN curl -fsSL https://example.com/app.tgz | tar xz -C /opt
```

After:

```dockerfile
SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-o", "pipefail", "-c"]
RUN curl -fsSL https://example.com/app.tgz | tar xz -C /opt
```

## DD045

**Package install without -y will hang or fail the build**  
`missing-yes` · error · correctness · Dockerfile · auto-fixable

apt-get, yum and dnf ask "Do you want to continue? [Y/n]" unless you pass -y. There is no terminal during a build to answer.

**Why it matters.** The build aborts with "E: Abort." (or waits forever in some CI setups) the first time it runs on a clean cache.

Before:

```dockerfile
RUN apt-get install curl
```

After:

```dockerfile
RUN apt-get install -y curl
```

## DD046

**RUN starts with cd instead of using WORKDIR**  
`cd-in-run` · info · maintainability · Dockerfile

A RUN begins with `cd <dir> &&`.

**Why it matters.** The directory change only lasts for that RUN, and the next instruction starts back in the old directory. WORKDIR makes the location explicit and persistent.

Before:

```dockerfile
RUN cd /app && npm ci
```

After:

```dockerfile
WORKDIR /app
RUN npm ci
```

## DC000

**Compose file is not valid YAML**  
`invalid-yaml` · error · correctness · compose file

The file could not be parsed as YAML, so none of the other compose rules could run.

**Why it matters.** docker compose refuses to start. Tabs for indentation and unquoted special characters are the usual culprits.

Before:

```yaml
services:
	web:
		image: nginx:1.27
```

After:

```yaml
services:
  web:
    image: nginx:1.27
```

## DC001

**Service image has no tag or uses :latest**  
`compose-unpinned-image` · warn · reproducibility · compose file

A pulled service image is untagged or tagged :latest. Services that are built locally (build:) are ignored.

**Why it matters.** Next `docker compose pull` can bring a new major version of your database or proxy, and a restart on another machine can run something different from what you tested.

Before:

```yaml
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:latest
```

After:

```yaml
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16.4-alpine
```

## DC002

**privileged: true**  
`compose-privileged` · error · security · compose file

The service runs with full access to host devices and almost all kernel capabilities.

**Why it matters.** A privileged container can mount the host disk, load kernel modules and escape with trivial effort. Grant the single capability or device you need with cap_add or devices.

Before:

```yaml
services:
  app:
    privileged: true
```

After:

```yaml
services:
  app:
    cap_add: [NET_ADMIN]
```

## DC003

**Docker socket mounted into a container**  
`compose-docker-socket` · error · security · compose file

A volume mounts /var/run/docker.sock (or any docker.sock) into the service. Mounting it read-only does not help.

**Why it matters.** Whoever controls that socket controls the Docker daemon, which means root on the host: they can start a privileged container that mounts "/". If you need it (CI runner, reverse proxy), put a socket proxy with a restricted API in front.

Before:

```yaml
services:
  proxy:
    volumes:
      - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro
```

After:

```yaml
services:
  proxy:
    environment:
      DOCKER_HOST: tcp://socket-proxy:2375
```

## DC004

**network_mode: host**  
`compose-host-network` · warn · security · compose file

The container shares the host network stack.

**Why it matters.** Network isolation is gone: the container can reach services bound to localhost on the host and can bind any host port. It also does not work on Docker Desktop for Mac and Windows. Publish the ports you need instead.

Before:

```yaml
services:
  app:
    network_mode: host
```

After:

```yaml
services:
  app:
    ports: ["127.0.0.1:8080:8080"]
```

## DC005

**Database port published on all interfaces**  
`compose-db-port-public` · error · security · compose file

A database or cache port (Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB, Redis, Elasticsearch, ...) is published without binding to 127.0.0.1.

**Why it matters.** Docker edits iptables itself, so `ports: "5432:5432"` bypasses ufw and most host firewalls and exposes the database to the whole network. Bind to loopback, or do not publish at all and let other services reach it over the compose network.

Before:

```yaml
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"
```

After:

```yaml
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:5432:5432"
```

## DC006

**Secret written literally in environment:**  
`compose-secret-in-environment` · error · security · compose file

An environment entry has a secret-looking name with a literal value (warning), or a value that matches a known credential format or looks like a random token (error). Values taken from the shell or an env_file (${VAR}) are fine.

**Why it matters.** The compose file is committed to git, so the secret is too. Use ${VAR} interpolation from an untracked .env, Docker secrets (secrets: + *_FILE variables), or your platform's secret store.

Before:

```yaml
services:
  db:
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: s3cr3t-prod-pass
```

After:

```yaml
services:
  db:
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE: /run/secrets/db_password
    secrets: [db_password]
```

## DC007

**Service has no restart policy**  
`compose-no-restart` · info · correctness · compose file

No restart: (or deploy.restart_policy) is set. Services in a profile and services named like one-shot jobs (migrate, init, seed, setup) are skipped.

**Why it matters.** After a crash or a host reboot the service stays down until someone notices. `restart: unless-stopped` is the usual choice for long-running services.

Before:

```yaml
services:
  web:
    image: nginx:1.27
```

After:

```yaml
services:
  web:
    image: nginx:1.27
    restart: unless-stopped
```

## DC008

**Service has no healthcheck**  
`compose-no-healthcheck` · info · correctness · compose file

The service defines no healthcheck (and the image may not either). Services in a profile and one-shot jobs are skipped.

**Why it matters.** Without a healthcheck, `depends_on: condition: service_healthy` is unavailable and `docker ps` reports a hung process as "Up".

Before:

```yaml
services:
  api:
    image: myorg/api:1.4.2
```

After:

```yaml
services:
  api:
    image: myorg/api:1.4.2
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "wget", "-qO-", "http://127.0.0.1:8080/health"]
      interval: 30s
```

## DC009

**No CPU or memory limits**  
`compose-no-resource-limits` · info · reproducibility · compose file

The service sets no deploy.resources.limits, mem_limit or cpus.

**Why it matters.** One leaking container can take the whole host down, including its neighbours. Even a generous limit turns an outage into one restarted container.

Before:

```yaml
services:
  api:
    image: myorg/api:1.4.2
```

After:

```yaml
services:
  api:
    image: myorg/api:1.4.2
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits: { cpus: "1.0", memory: 512M }
```

## DC010

**depends_on waits for start, not for health**  
`compose-depends-on-no-condition` · info · correctness · compose file

A service depends on another service that has a healthcheck, but depends_on does not use condition: service_healthy.

**Why it matters.** "Started" is not "ready": the database container is up several seconds before it accepts connections, so the app crashes on boot and relies on restarts to recover. A healthcheck already exists; use it.

Before:

```yaml
services:
  db:
    healthcheck: { test: ["CMD", "pg_isready"] }
  api:
    depends_on: [db]
```

After:

```yaml
services:
  api:
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
```

## DC011

**Dangerous capabilities or security profiles disabled**  
`compose-dangerous-capabilities` · warn · security · compose file

cap_add contains ALL, SYS_ADMIN, SYS_MODULE, SYS_PTRACE, SYS_RAWIO or DAC_READ_SEARCH, or security_opt switches off seccomp/AppArmor/SELinux labelling.

**Why it matters.** These are the building blocks of container escapes. SYS_ADMIN alone is close to being privileged. Add only the narrow capability you can name a reason for.

Before:

```yaml
services:
  app:
    cap_add: [SYS_ADMIN]
    security_opt: ["seccomp=unconfined"]
```

After:

```yaml
services:
  app:
    cap_add: [NET_BIND_SERVICE]
```

## DC012

**Container shares a host namespace (pid / ipc / uts / userns)**  
`compose-host-namespaces` · warn · security · compose file

pid: host, ipc: host, uts: host or userns_mode: host is set.

**Why it matters.** The container can see and signal every process on the host (pid), or read shared memory of other workloads (ipc). Isolation is the point of a container.

Before:

```yaml
services:
  agent:
    pid: host
```

After:

```yaml
services:
  agent:
    # remove pid: host, or isolate the agent on a dedicated host
```

## DC013

**Service forced to run as root**  
`compose-root-user` · warn · security · compose file

user: root, user: "0" or user: "0:0" overrides the image's own USER.

**Why it matters.** It undoes whatever non-root user the image went to the trouble of setting up. Prefer a numeric non-root uid and fix file ownership instead.

Before:

```yaml
services:
  app:
    user: root
```

After:

```yaml
services:
  app:
    user: "10001:10001"
```

## DC014

**Top-level `version:` is obsolete**  
`compose-obsolete-version` · info · maintainability · compose file · auto-fixable

The Compose Specification ignores the top-level version field, and Compose v2 prints a warning for it.

**Why it matters.** It suggests a schema version that no longer exists and can mislead readers about which features are available. --fix removes the line.

Before:

```yaml
version: "3.8"
services: {}
```

After:

```yaml
services: {}
```

## DC015

**Fixed container_name prevents scaling and clashes between projects**  
`compose-container-name` · info · maintainability · compose file

container_name pins a global name for the container.

**Why it matters.** Two projects (or two copies of the same project) cannot run side by side, and `docker compose up --scale` fails. Compose already gives containers stable, project-scoped names.

Before:

```yaml
services:
  web:
    container_name: web
```

After:

```yaml
services:
  web:
    image: nginx:1.27
```
